newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Kohan hits back at Cavallo accusations.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Kohan hits back at Cavallo accusations.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem's chief of staff, Alberto Kohan, hit back Wednesday against accusations made against him by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo.
"What I want is for people who lie to be punished," Kohan was quoted as saying by the private DyN news agency. He said he was considering suing Cavallo, but a final decision "depends on the lawyers."
Cavallo, who has embarked on a fierce anti-corruption drive since being fired by Menem in July, had earlier in the day called Kohan a "criminal."
On other occasions, Cavallo has alleged that Kohan knew of, but failed to act against, bribes paid to win a $250 million contract with the state-owned Banco Nacion.
In his remarks to DyN, Kohan also dismissed charges by Cavallo that the former head of the customs service, Gustavo Parino, had been falsely arrested.
Cavallo had said that Parino, who was arrested early Wednesday, was a "political prisoner," an emotive term dating from the time of Argentina's military governments.
"Luckily, thank God, in today's Argentina there are no political prisoners," Kohan said.

Earlier this week, Cavallo said that both he and Parino were the targets of persecution by the courts, which he claimed were being manipulated by crime rings who were trying to protect themselves from his campaign against corruption.
Since his dismissal by Menem, Cavallo has peppered the government and judiciary with accusations of graft and has been enmeshed in a series of court cases for his comments.

Cavallo has launched himself as an alternative political force, focusing on a crusade against corruption. But he has played down the likelihood he will stage a bid for the nation's presidency in 1999.
Cavallo was involved in a confused incident Wednesday when he arrived at his Buenos Aires home to be faced by a group of protestors, who accused him of him of being corrupt.
But one of the protestors later told a local radio station that he had been sent to demonstrate by officials of the governing Peronist Party.
